LETTER TO THE EDITOR
Vascular small fiber neuropathy in neuronal intranuclear
inclusion disease
Dear Editor,
We were interested in the recent study by Liu et al., which analyzed
cutaneous small nerve fibers of participants with neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease (NIID), Parkinson’s disease (PD), Alzheimer’s
disease (AD), and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN). Their findings
revealed widespread and severe small fiber neuropathy (SFN) in
NIID, characterized by a non-length-dependent reduction in intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) and the density of sudomotor
and pilomotor nerve fibers. IENFD demonstrated high diagnostic
accuracy in distinguishing NIID from healthy controls (HCs) and other
diseases.1
They identified sweat gland and pilomotor small fiber damage
in the distal leg, proximal thigh, and cervical skin.1 However, nerve
pathology in the distal forearm, particularly in the perivascular region,
remained unexamined. To address this gap, we conducted a complementary study, recruiting patients with NIID and age-/sex-matched
HCs from the Department of Neurology, Affiliated Zhongda Hospital of Southeast University (August 2021–April 2024), with ethical
approval (2024ZDSYLL331-P01). Inclusion and exclusion criteria, clinical assessments, intranuclear inclusion frequency, IENFD quantification, and statistical methods followed those outlined by Liu et al.1
Participants underwent cardiovascular autonomic testing, evaluating
parasympathetic function (via heart rate responses to deep breathing
and the Valsalva maneuver) and sympathetic function (via blood pressure responses during the Valsalva maneuver).2 Skin biopsies from the
distal forearm were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, and 50 µm frozen
sections were prepared for immunofluorescence staining. In addition
to the primary antibodies used by Liu et al.1 against the pan-neuronal
marker protein gene product 9.5 (PGP 9.5), collagen type IV, tyrosine

hydroxylase (TH), and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), we employed
antibodies against dopamine β-hydroxylase (Rabbit DβH, 1:200, Cat#
22806, ImmunoStar) for adrenergic fibers and p62/SQSTM1 (Rabbit,
1:1000, Cat# P0067, Sigma-Aldrich) for intranuclear inclusions. Confocal Z-stack images (30 µm) of each vessel and sweat gland were
analyzed automatically and blindly, following the methods described by
Vincenzo and Gibbons.2–4 Nerve fiber density (FD) was calculated as
the ratio of nerve fiber area to vessel wall or sweat gland area, whereas
fiber length (FL) was measured as the Feret diameter along the fiber
axis (in micrometers).3

We included 24 patients with NIID (median age 66.0 years,
interquartile range [IQR] 63.25–70.00) and 24 matched HCs (median
age 67.00 years, IQR 60.25–72.75) (Tables S1, S2, Figure S1). NIID
patients exhibited marked perivascular nerve damage, with significantly reduced FD and FL of vascular pan-neural, noradrenergic,
adrenergic, and cholinergic fibers, alongside lower positivity rates
for adrenergic and cholinergic fibers (all p < 0.05) (Figure 1, Table
S3). Consistent with Liu et al., we observed impaired IENFD and
sudomotor innervation, reflected in reduced sudomotor pan-neural,
noradrenergic, and cholinergic nerve FD, as well as decreased cholinergic fiber positivity (all p < 0.05) (Figure S2, S3 and Table S3).

Notably, intranuclear inclusion frequency correlated negatively with
sudomotor noradrenergic FD (r = −0.54, p = 0.03) and FL (r = −0.50,
p = 0.045), suggesting selective noradrenergic vulnerability. These
findings expand upon the work of Liu et al. and offer new insights into
the pathophysiology of peripheral neuropathy in NIID.
Liu et al. demonstrated that IENFD effectively distinguishes NIID
from PD, AD, DPN, and HCs, but its reduction is non-specific in multiple
disorders. As intranuclear inclusions and NOTCH2NLC testing remain
the established diagnostic standard, IENFD should be combined with
other examinations in clinical practice, requiring multicenter validation
to enhance diagnostic accuracy and minimize potential bias.
SFN in NIID may sometimes present with subtle clinical symptoms.5
In Case P7, for instance, the initial symptom was mild urinary frequency. Approximately half of patients with NIID exhibit subclinical
peripheral neuropathy,6–8 underscoring the diagnostic importance of
early SFN recognition and the consideration of NIID. Clinical features
such as orthostatic hypotension and cutaneous flushing are strongly
associated with impaired vasomotor function, indicating detailed characterization of vascular nerve subtypes may inform targeted therapeutic approaches. Methodologically, we employed automated quantification to assess vascular innervation, minimizing the confounding
effects from vessel orientation and thickness by selecting circular vessel walls as regions of interest and transverse sections. Although this
method is less precise than stereological quantification, especially in
mild cases with axonal hypertrophy, Gibbons et al. demonstrated automated quantification correlates well with stereological assessment of
sudomotor innervation (r = 0.76, p < 0.05), and had superior efficiency and reproducibility.4 Our study is not as comprehensive as that

nerve fibers in NIID patients compared to HCs, specifically in pan-neural (A, B), noradrenergic (C, D), adrenergic (E, F), and cholinergic (G, H)
subtypes. Quantitative measurements confirmed a significant decrease in FD and FL for these types of fibers, along with reduced positivity rates

of Liu et al., however, our findings provide complementary pathological evidence of SFN in NIID. Future research should aim to elucidate
the mechanistic relationships between vascular pathology and core
clinical manifestations, such as dementia, cerebral small vessel disease, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction, which may unveil promising
therapeutic targets.
